$comment: Threads (Phase 4, P4.2). The seed connections from docs/PLAN.md §14 as OSIS references in WEBC (English) numbering, each with an original explanation and its citations: OpenBible.info cross-reference rows, words the WEBC text itself carries at a verse (checked at build), shared Greek words at their Septuagint and TAGNT rows (checked by `pnpm connections:verify`), and, for every interpretive reading, a Church Father's work and section in a pinned public-domain edition with a phrase that must occur there. Where the plan names several passages, each is its own connection; the plan's 'Exodus (whole)' is anchored at Exod 19:1, where the Septuagint uses the word Luke 9:31 shares, and 'Genesis–Kings' at Abraham's call through the temple's dedication. P4.4 adds connections book by book from the candidate pool (`pnpm connections:propose <bookId>`, docs/connections/<bookId>-candidates.md), with ids prefixed by the book. A connection is shown on the site only once it is `verified`, with the owner's approval carrying a fingerprint of its content.

connections.label: The overshadowing cloud of glory and the overshadowing of Mary
connections.explanation: When the tabernacle is finished, the cloud covers the tent and the LORD's glory fills it, so that even Moses cannot go in. In the Septuagint the cloud overshadows the tent with the same verb Gabriel uses when he tells Mary that the power of the Most High will overshadow her (both forms are below). Luke uses the verb again for the cloud at the Transfiguration.

connections.label: The overshadowing cloud of glory and the cloud at the Transfiguration
connections.explanation: On the mountain a cloud comes and overshadows the disciples, and they are afraid as they enter it, where Moses could not enter the tent the cloud had covered. Luke's Greek has the Septuagint's noun for the cloud and its verb for the overshadowing (below). Moses himself is one of the two men speaking with Jesus.

connections.label: The Shema as the greatest commandment
connections.explanation: Asked what is written in the law about inheriting eternal life, a lawyer answers with Deuteronomy's command to love the LORD with all one's heart, soul and strength, joined to the command from Leviticus to love one's neighbour as oneself. Jesus tells him he has answered correctly. Luke's wording adds the mind to Deuteronomy's three.

connections.label: Hannah's song and the Magnificat
connections.explanation: Two women sing of a son God has given beyond expectation: Hannah when she brings Samuel to the LORD's house at Shiloh, Mary when she visits Elizabeth after the angel's promise. Both songs praise God for overturning the order of things, bringing down the mighty, lifting up the lowly and filling the hungry. Both WEBC texts speak of princes, and in the Greek the word is the same (below).

connections.label: A widow's son raised and given back to his mother
connections.explanation: Elijah meets the widow of Zarephath at the gate of her city and later raises her son; Jesus meets a widow at the gate of Nain as her only son is carried out, and raises him. Both stories close on the same act, the son handed back to his mother, and in Greek Luke's five closing words are the Septuagint's five words for Elijah's act (below). The crowd at Nain responds by calling Jesus a great prophet.

connections.label: Jesus cites the widow of Zarephath at Nazareth
connections.explanation: In the synagogue at Nazareth Jesus recalls the famine in Elijah's days and the widow of Zarephath in Sidon, a foreigner to whom the prophet was sent while the many widows in Israel were not. He names her in answer to a town that expects him to do at home what he did at Capernaum.

connections.label: Jesus cites Naaman at Nazareth
connections.explanation: In the same breath Jesus names Naaman the Syrian, the army commander made clean of leprosy when he dipped himself in the Jordan at Elisha's word, though there were many lepers in Israel. Both of the examples he gives at Nazareth are foreigners.

connections.label: Fire from heaven called down, then refused
connections.explanation: When a Samaritan village will not receive Jesus, James and John offer to command fire to come down from the sky, and they name Elijah, who called it down on the king's captains and their men. Jesus turns and rebukes them. In Kings the fire falls; in Luke it is refused.

connections.label: A master taken up; his spirit passes to the disciples
connections.explanation: Elijah is taken up while Elisha watches, and the prophets at Jericho see that Elijah's spirit now rests on his disciple. In Acts Jesus is taken up while the apostles watch, and at Pentecost they are filled with the Holy Spirit. The Septuagint and Acts use the same verb for the master being taken up (below). Chrysostom sets the two partings side by side: the angels come, he says, so that the apostles will not grieve as Elisha did when he tore his clothes.

sources.author: John Chrysostom
sources.work: Homilies on the Acts of the Apostles
sources.heading: Homily II.
sources.phrase: that it might not be with them as it was with Elisha

connections.label: A crowd fed from little, with food left over
connections.explanation: A man brings Elisha twenty barley loaves; his servant asks how so little can be set before a hundred men, yet they eat and some is left over. In Luke the twelve object that they have only five loaves and two fish for about five thousand men, and after all have eaten, twelve baskets of pieces remain. Both stories turn on the same objection and end with food to spare.

connections.label: Babel's confusion of languages undone at Pentecost
connections.explanation: At Babel the one language is confused and its speakers are scattered over the earth; at Pentecost people from every nation gather in Jerusalem and each hears the apostles in his own language. The Septuagint's verb for the confusion at Babel is the verb Acts uses for the bewildered crowd (below). Augustine and Chrysostom both read Pentecost against Babel: for Augustine, Christ's humility gathers the tongues that pride divided.

sources.author: Augustine
sources.work: Tractates on the Gospel of John
sources.heading: Tractate VI.
sources.phrase: If pride caused diversities of tongues, Christ's humility has united these diversities in one

sources.author: John Chrysostom
sources.heading: Homily XXXV.
sources.phrase: as in the time of building the tower the one tongue was divided into many

connections.label: The beloved son
connections.explanation: When God tells Abraham to offer Isaac, the Septuagint names Isaac with the adjective the voice from the sky uses at Jesus' baptism for the beloved Son (both forms are below). WEBC, translating the Hebrew, has Abraham's only son, whom he loves. The voice uses the same word again at the Transfiguration.

connections.label: Passover at the Last Supper
connections.explanation: Luke sets the Last Supper on the day the Passover lamb was sacrificed, and Jesus tells the twelve he has longed to eat this Passover with them before he suffers. Exodus 12 commands the lamb, its blood on the doorposts and a meal kept as a memorial through the generations; at the supper Jesus gives the bread and tells them to do this in memory of him. Tertullian notes that of all the feasts Jesus chose the Passover for his suffering, and Chrysostom says that where the type was, Christ set the truth.

sources.author: Tertullian
sources.heading: Chapter XL.
sources.phrase: of all the festal days of the Jews He chose the passover

sources.author: John Chrysostom
sources.work: Homilies on the Gospel of Matthew
sources.heading: Homily LXXXII.
sources.phrase: where the type is, there He puts the truth

connections.label: The blood of the covenant at the Last Supper
connections.explanation: At Sinai Moses seals the covenant by sprinkling the people with blood and calling it the blood of the covenant. Over the cup after supper Jesus speaks of the new covenant in his blood, poured out for the disciples. Commenting on the same words in Matthew, Chrysostom says Jesus recalls the former covenant because it too was dedicated with blood.

sources.author: John Chrysostom
sources.work: Homilies on the Gospel of Matthew
sources.heading: Homily LXXXII.
sources.phrase: for that also was dedicated with blood

connections.label: The sign of Jonah
connections.explanation: Asked for a sign, Jesus says his generation will be given none but the sign of Jonah: as Jonah was a sign to the Ninevites, so the Son of Man will be to them. He recalls that Nineveh repented at Jonah's preaching, as Jonah 3 tells, and says that one greater than Jonah is here.

connections.label: The throne of David promised to Mary's son
connections.explanation: Through Nathan, God promises David an heir whose throne and kingdom will be established forever. Gabriel tells Mary that the Lord God will give her son the throne of his father David, and that his kingdom will have no end. The angel's message takes up the promise's own terms: throne, kingdom, forever.

connections.label: A companion on the road, unrecognised (proposed)
connections.explanation: Tobias looks for a companion for his journey and finds Raphael, an angel, without knowing it; the angel offers to go with him and knows the way. On the road to Emmaus Jesus comes near and walks with two disciples whose eyes are kept from recognising him, and he opens the Scriptures to them on the way. The Greek verb for going along with someone appears in both (below). This parallel is proposed by the plan; it is not in the cross-reference data.

connections.label: A companion revealed, then gone (proposed)
connections.explanation: At the journey's end Raphael tells Tobit and Tobias who he is, says he is going up to the one who sent him, and they see him no more. At Emmaus the two disciples recognise Jesus as he breaks the bread, and he vanishes from their sight. In both, the companion is known only at the end and is gone at once. This parallel is proposed by the plan; it is not in the cross-reference data.

connections.label: The feast of Dedication
connections.explanation: John places Jesus in the temple at Jerusalem in winter, at the Feast of the Dedication. 1 Maccabees 4 tells how that feast began: after the temple was profaned, Judas and his kindred cleansed it, dedicated the new altar, and ordained that the dedication be kept every year for eight days from the twenty-fifth of Chislev.

connections.label: Jesus' coming exodus in Jerusalem
connections.explanation: At the Transfiguration Moses and Elijah speak with Jesus about the departure he is about to accomplish at Jerusalem. Luke's Greek word for that departure is the noun the Septuagint uses at Sinai for Israel's going out of Egypt (below), and Moses, who led that going out, is one of the two speaking with him.

connections.label: Jesus reads his programme from Isaiah
connections.explanation: In the synagogue at Nazareth Jesus is handed the book of the prophet Isaiah and reads the passage now numbered Isaiah 61: one anointed by the Spirit to bring good news to the poor, release to captives and the year of the LORD's favour. He then tells his hearers that this Scripture has been fulfilled in their hearing. His reading stops before Isaiah's day of vengeance.

connections.label: The Son of Man on the clouds
connections.explanation: Speaking of the end, Jesus foretells the Son of Man's coming in a cloud, with power and great glory. The words take up Daniel's night vision of one like a son of man coming with the clouds to the Ancient of Days, who is given dominion, glory and a kingdom. Both Greek versions of Daniel have the noun Luke uses for the cloud (below).

connections.label: The Son of Man at the right hand of power
connections.explanation: Before the council Jesus declares that the Son of Man will from now on be seated at the right hand of God's power. The title comes from Daniel's vision, where one like a son of man is brought before the Ancient of Days and given dominion; the seat at the right hand recalls the first verse of Psalm 110.

connections.label: Stephen retells the whole story you have read
connections.explanation: Brought before the council, Stephen answers by retelling Israel's story: God's call to Abraham in Mesopotamia, Joseph sold into Egypt, Moses, the tabernacle in the wilderness, Joshua and David, and Solomon building a house for God. It is the ground the path has covered from Genesis to Kings, told as a single speech.

connections.label: In the beginning
connections.explanation: John's Gospel opens with the words that open Genesis, in the beginning, and then speaks of the Word who was with God. Where Genesis says God created the heavens and the earth, John says all things were made through the Word and nothing was made without him.

connections.label: God rested on the seventh day
connections.explanation: Hebrews quotes Genesis on God resting on the seventh day from all his works, as part of its argument that a Sabbath rest still remains for the people of God. The Greek of Hebrews keeps the Septuagint's verb for resting and its word for the seventh (below).

connections.label: Male and female; the two become one flesh
connections.explanation: Asked about divorce, Jesus answers from the first chapters of Genesis: the Creator made them male and female, and a man leaves his father and mother and is joined to his wife, so that the two become one flesh. He draws his own conclusion from them, that no one should separate what God has joined.

connections.label: The two become one flesh
connections.explanation: Ephesians quotes the verse from Genesis about a man leaving his father and mother to be joined to his wife, the two becoming one flesh. It then calls this a great mystery and applies it to Christ and the assembly, the Church.

connections.label: The first man Adam became a living soul
connections.explanation: In Genesis the LORD God forms man from the dust and breathes life into him, and man becomes a living soul. Paul cites the verse as written Scripture, names the first man as Adam, and sets beside him a last Adam who became a life-giving spirit.

connections.label: He breathed on them
connections.explanation: In the Septuagint, God breathes life into the first man with the verb John uses the same rare verb when the risen Jesus breathes on his disciples and tells them to receive the Holy Spirit (both forms are below). The New Testament uses the verb nowhere else.

connections.label: As the serpent deceived Eve
connections.explanation: Genesis tells how the serpent, more subtle than any animal of the field, led the woman to eat, and how she said that the serpent had deceived her. Paul names Eve and the serpent's craftiness as the pattern he fears for the Corinthians, that their minds might be led away from Christ.

connections.label: The blood of Abel
connections.explanation: Cain kills his brother Abel in the field, and the LORD says that Abel's blood cries to him from the ground. Jesus names Abel as the first in the line of the righteous whose blood was shed, from Abel to Zechariah, and warns that it will be required of his generation.

connections.label: Enoch taken by God
connections.explanation: Genesis says only that Enoch walked with God and was not found, because God took him. Hebrews names Enoch among the examples of faith, saying he was taken away without seeing death and had pleased God, and like Genesis it says that he was not found.

connections.label: As it was in the days of Noah
connections.explanation: Speaking of the day the Son of Man is revealed, Jesus compares it to the days of Noah: people ate, drank and married until Noah entered the ark and the flood came and destroyed them all. Luke's Greek uses the Septuagint's words for the ark and the flood (below).

connections.label: The days of Lot; remember Lot's wife
connections.explanation: In the same teaching Jesus recalls the days of Lot, when fire and sulfur rained on Sodom on the day Lot went out, and he tells his hearers to remember Lot's wife, who in Genesis looked back and became a pillar of salt. The warning that follows is not to turn back.

connections.label: Melchizedek, king of Salem
connections.explanation: Genesis gives Melchizedek three verses: king of Salem and priest of God Most High, he brings bread and wine, blesses Abram, and receives a tenth of all. Hebrews retells the meeting, explains what his name and title mean, and describes him as without father, mother or genealogy.

connections.label: Abraham believed God
connections.explanation: Genesis says that Abram believed the LORD, who counted it to him as righteousness. Paul quotes the verse as what Scripture says and makes it the centre of his argument that Abraham was counted righteous through faith; his Greek keeps the Septuagint's words for counting it and for righteousness (below).

connections.label: In you all the nations will be blessed
connections.explanation: When God calls Abram, he promises that all the families of the earth will be blessed through him. Paul quotes the promise and says that Scripture announced the good news to Abraham in advance, foreseeing that God would justify the nations by faith.

connections.label: All the families of the earth will be blessed
connections.explanation: After the binding of Isaac, God repeats his promise that all the nations of the earth will be blessed through Abraham's offspring. At the temple in Jerusalem, Peter quotes it to the crowd as the covenant God made with their fathers, and the Greek verb for the blessing is the Septuagint's (below).

connections.label: Nothing is impossible for God
connections.explanation: When Sarah laughs at the promise of a son in her old age, the LORD asks whether anything is too hard for him. Gabriel tells Mary that her aged relative Elizabeth, called barren, has conceived, and that nothing spoken by God is impossible; Luke's verb is the Septuagint's in Genesis 18:14, rare in the New Testament (below).

connections.label: Cast out the servant and her son
connections.explanation: Sarah tells Abraham to cast out the servant Hagar and her son, so that he will not inherit with Isaac, and God tells Abraham to listen to her. Paul quotes her words as Scripture and reads the two women, the slave and the free, as two covenants, saying himself that these things contain an allegory.

connections.label: Abraham offers Isaac
connections.explanation: Genesis tells how God tested Abraham by asking him to offer Isaac, and stopped his hand. Hebrews names the test as an act of faith: Abraham offered his only son, through whom the promise was to come, reasoning that God could raise him even from the dead.

connections.label: Angels ascending and descending
connections.explanation: At Bethel Jacob dreams of a stairway reaching to heaven with the angels of God ascending and descending on it. Jesus promises Nathanael a sight of heaven opened, with those same angels going up and coming down on the Son of Man; in Greek the angels and both verbs are the Septuagint's (below).

connections.label: The elder will serve the younger
connections.explanation: When Rebekah's children struggle within her, the LORD tells her that two nations are in her womb and that the elder will serve the younger. Paul names Rebekah and quotes the oracle to argue that God's choice rests on his call, not on what the children had done.

connections.label: God has taken away my reproach
connections.explanation: When God remembers Rachel and opens her womb, she bears a son and says that God has taken away her reproach. When Elizabeth conceives, she says the Lord has looked on her to take away her reproach among people, and Luke's word for reproach, found nowhere else in the New Testament, is the Septuagint's in Rachel's words (below).

connections.label: He did not spare his own son
connections.explanation: The angel tells Abraham that he has not withheld his only son. Paul writes that God did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all, using the verb the Septuagint uses in the angel's words to Abraham (below).

connections.label: He takes the wise in their craftiness
connections.explanation: Eliphaz tells Job that God takes the wise in their own craftiness and frustrates the plans of the cunning. Paul quotes the line as written Scripture to show that the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God; in Greek both have the same word for the wise (below).

connections.label: The endurance of Job
connections.explanation: Having lost his children and everything he owned, Job blesses the name of the LORD, and Job 1 notes that in all this he did not sin. James names Job as the example of perseverance and of the Lord's compassion in the outcome; it is the only place the New Testament names him (below).

connections.label: Ways past tracing out
connections.explanation: Job says that God does great things past finding out and wonders without number. Paul ends his long argument in Romans with praise of God's unsearchable judgements and ways past tracing out, using the Septuagint's adjective from Job 9:10, which the New Testament has only twice (below).

connections.label: Who has first given to him?
connections.explanation: At the end of the LORD's speeches from the whirlwind, God asks who has first given to him that he should repay. Paul closes the same hymn of praise in Romans with the question who has first given to God and will be repaid, close to the wording WEBC gives Job 41:11.

connections.label: This will turn out for my salvation
connections.explanation: Job, defending himself before God, says that this will be his salvation. Writing from prison, Paul says he knows that this will turn out for his salvation; in Greek his words are the Septuagint's in Job 13:16, with a verb the New Testament has only four times (below).

connections.label: Naked I came, naked I return
connections.explanation: On losing everything, Job says that he came naked from his mother's womb and will return there naked, and blesses the LORD's name. First Timothy makes the same observation about possessions, that we brought nothing into the world and can carry nothing out, as a ground for contentment.

connections.label: The adversary walking the earth
connections.explanation: In Job the adversary, Satan, comes before the LORD from going back and forth on the earth and walking up and down in it, and then strikes Job. First Peter warns that the adversary, the devil, walks around like a roaring lion; the Septuagint of Job calls Satan by the same Greek name, the devil (below).

connections.label: The lowly lifted up
connections.explanation: Eliphaz praises the God who sets on high those who are low. Mary's song praises God for exalting the lowly, and the Greek for the lowly is the same word in Luke and in the Septuagint of Job 5:11 (below).

connections.label: Moses at the bush
connections.explanation: Answering the Sadducees about the resurrection, Jesus points to the passage about the bush, where God calls himself the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob long after their deaths. Luke's Greek word for the bush is the Septuagint's in Exodus 3 (below).

connections.label: Stephen retells the burning bush
connections.explanation: In his speech before the council Stephen retells the call of Moses: the angel in the flame of fire in a bush, the God of the fathers, the command to take off his sandals, and God's word that he has seen his people's affliction in Egypt. The last of these follows Exodus 3:7 closely, with the Septuagint's rare word for affliction (below).

connections.label: Stephen recalls the golden calf
connections.explanation: While Moses delays on the mountain, the people ask Aaron to make them gods to go before them, and he makes a calf. Stephen quotes their demand to Aaron nearly word for word and tells how they sacrificed to the idol and rejoiced in the works of their hands.

connections.label: Every firstborn male holy to the Lord
connections.explanation: Exodus commands that every firstborn that opens the womb be set apart for the LORD. When Mary and Joseph present Jesus in the temple, Luke cites this as written in the law of the Lord, in the Septuagint's words for opening the womb (below).

connections.label: Not a bone broken
connections.explanation: Among the rules for the Passover lamb, Exodus says that none of its bones may be broken. John says that the soldiers did not break the legs of Jesus so that this Scripture would be fulfilled, and his Greek has the Septuagint's words for bone and breaking (below).

connections.label: You know the commandments
connections.explanation: When a ruler asks what he must do to inherit eternal life, Jesus lists commandments from the Decalogue: adultery, murder, theft, false testimony, and honouring father and mother. The Greek verbs for murder and theft are the Septuagint's (below).

connections.label: The first commandment with a promise
connections.explanation: Exodus gives the command to honour father and mother with a promise of long days in the land. Ephesians quotes it, calls it the first commandment with a promise, and keeps the Septuagint's wording for the promise, including a word for long life found nowhere else in the New Testament (below).

connections.label: For this purpose I raised you up
connections.explanation: Before the plague of hail, God tells Pharaoh that he has made him stand in order to show his power and have his name declared in all the earth. Paul quotes the words as what Scripture says to Pharaoh, with the Septuagint's verb for proclaiming the name (below).

connections.label: I will have mercy on whom I have mercy
connections.explanation: When Moses asks to see God's glory, the LORD says he will be gracious to whom he will be gracious and show mercy to whom he will show mercy. Paul quotes the saying as spoken to Moses, in the Septuagint's words for compassion (below).

connections.label: They sat down to eat and rose up to play
connections.explanation: At the golden calf the people offer sacrifices, sit down to eat and drink, and rise up to play. Paul quotes the verse as a warning against idolatry, and his verb for playing, found nowhere else in the New Testament, is the Septuagint's (below).

connections.label: The veil over Moses' face
connections.explanation: Coming down from Sinai, Moses' face shines, and he puts a veil over it when he has finished speaking to the people. Paul retells the scene, naming Moses and the veil, and contrasts that fading glory with the ministry of the Spirit; his word for the veil is the Septuagint's (below).

connections.label: A royal priesthood, a holy nation
connections.explanation: At Sinai God tells Israel that if they keep his covenant they will be his own possession, a kingdom of priests and a holy nation. First Peter gives these titles to its readers, and its word for a priesthood, which the New Testament has only twice, is the Septuagint's in Exodus 19:6 (below).

connections.label: The pattern shown on the mountain
connections.explanation: God tells Moses to make the tabernacle and its furnishings after the pattern shown to him on the mountain. Hebrews quotes the instruction and says the earthly sanctuary is a copy and shadow of the heavenly things.

connections.label: This is the blood of the covenant
connections.explanation: At Sinai Moses sprinkles the people with blood and calls it the blood of the covenant. Hebrews retells the rite, adding the book and the hyssop, and quotes Moses' words to show that the first covenant too was dedicated with blood.

connections.label: Manna in the wilderness
connections.explanation: In the wilderness God rains bread from heaven, and Israel calls it manna. After the feeding of the crowd, people remind Jesus that their fathers ate the manna in the wilderness; he answers that it was not Moses who gave them the bread from heaven, but his Father gives the true bread.

connections.label: By faith Moses
connections.explanation: Exodus 2 tells how Moses was hidden as a baby, raised as the son of Pharaoh's daughter, and fled after siding with his own people. Hebrews retells the same steps as acts of faith: his parents hid him, he refused to be called the son of Pharaoh's daughter, and he left Egypt.

connections.label: The song of Moses
connections.explanation: After the crossing of the sea, Moses and Israel sing to the LORD, who is glorious and does wonders. In Revelation those who have conquered sing the song of Moses and of the Lamb, praising God's marvellous works; Revelation's words for the song and for marvellous are the Septuagint's in Exodus 15 (below).

connections.label: As Moses lifted up the serpent
connections.explanation: When snakes bite the people in the wilderness, the LORD tells Moses to set a bronze serpent on a pole, and whoever looks at it lives. Speaking to Nicodemus, Jesus names this act of Moses and says the Son of Man must be lifted up in the same way; the serpent is the Septuagint's word (below).

connections.label: Bodies that fell in the wilderness
connections.explanation: After the spies' report, the LORD says that the bodies of the generation that grumbled will fall in the wilderness over forty years. Hebrews recalls those who came out of Egypt with Moses and whose bodies fell in the wilderness, with the Septuagint's word for their bodies, found nowhere else in the New Testament (below).

connections.label: The ashes of a heifer
connections.explanation: Numbers 19 prescribes a red heifer, burned outside the camp, whose ashes in water cleanse those made unclean. Hebrews names the ashes of a heifer that sanctify for the cleansing of the flesh, and its word for the heifer, found nowhere else in the New Testament, is the Septuagint's (below).

connections.label: Faithful in all his house
connections.explanation: When Miriam and Aaron speak against Moses, the LORD says that his servant Moses is faithful in all his house. Hebrews takes up the phrase twice, comparing Jesus with Moses, and keeps the Septuagint's word for a servant, which the New Testament has only here (below).

connections.label: Aaron's rod that budded
connections.explanation: To end the people's grumbling, Aaron's rod sprouts, buds and blossoms overnight in the tent, and the LORD tells Moses to keep it before the testimony. Hebrews lists Aaron's rod that budded among the things kept in the ark, with the Septuagint's verb for budding (below).

connections.label: The teaching of Balaam
connections.explanation: At Shittim Israel is drawn into immorality and the worship of the Baal of Peor, and Numbers later blames the counsel of Balaam for it. The letter to Pergamum in Revelation names Balaam, who taught Balak to put a stumbling block before Israel, to eat food sacrificed to idols and commit sexual immorality.

connections.label: Balaam's donkey
connections.explanation: Riding to curse Israel for Balak, Balaam is stopped by his donkey, whose mouth the LORD opens to speak to him. Second Peter names Balaam the son of Beor, who loved the wages of wrongdoing, and recalls the speechless donkey that spoke with a human voice; Balaam's name is spelled as in the Septuagint (below).

connections.label: Korah's rebellion
connections.explanation: Korah and his followers rise against Moses and Aaron, and the earth opens and swallows them. Jude names Korah's rebellion, with the way of Cain and the error of Balaam, as the fate of those he warns against.

connections.label: They craved evil things
connections.explanation: In the wilderness the people crave meat and complain, and the place where those who craved were buried is named for their craving. Paul says these things happened as examples so that we would not crave evil things as they did; his word for those who crave, found nowhere else in the New Testament, is the Septuagint's in Numbers 11:34 (below).

connections.label: Seventy sent out
connections.explanation: Moses is told to gather seventy elders, and the LORD puts on them some of the Spirit that was on Moses. Luke tells how the Lord appointed seventy others and sent them out two by two; the number in Greek is the Septuagint's in Numbers 11 (below).

connections.label: Not by bread alone
connections.explanation: Moses reminds Israel that God fed them with manna in the wilderness to teach them that a person does not live by bread alone. Tempted in the wilderness to turn a stone into bread, Jesus answers with this verse as what is written.

connections.label: Worship the Lord your God
connections.explanation: Deuteronomy tells Israel to fear the LORD and serve him. When the devil offers Jesus the kingdoms of the world in return for worship, Jesus answers with this command as what is written; the verb for serving is the Septuagint's (below).

connections.label: Do not put the Lord your God to the test
connections.explanation: Moses warns Israel not to test the LORD as they did at Massah. When the devil sets Jesus on the pinnacle of the temple and invites him to throw himself down, Jesus answers with this command, in the Septuagint's verb for testing (below).

connections.label: A prophet like me
connections.explanation: Moses promises that the LORD will raise up a prophet like him from among the people, and that they must listen to him. Peter quotes the promise to the crowd at the temple as Moses' own words and applies it to Jesus.

connections.label: Stephen recalls the promised prophet
connections.explanation: In his speech to the council Stephen recalls that the same Moses who led the people out of Egypt told them God would raise up a prophet like him. He quotes the promise from Deuteronomy as part of his account of how the people rejected those God sent.

connections.label: Do not muzzle the ox
connections.explanation: Among the laws of Deuteronomy is that an ox treading grain must not be muzzled. Paul quotes it as written in the law of Moses to argue that those who work for the gospel may live by it, and asks whether God's concern is really for oxen.

connections.label: Cursed is everyone who does not keep the law
connections.explanation: The curses spoken from Mount Ebal end with a curse on whoever does not uphold the words of the law by doing them. Paul quotes it as written to argue that those who rely on the works of the law are under a curse; the words for cursed and for abiding are the Septuagint's (below).

connections.label: The word is near you
connections.explanation: Moses tells Israel that the commandment is not in heaven or beyond the sea, but very near, in their mouth and in their heart. Paul quotes these lines, interpreting the going up to heaven and down to the abyss as about Christ, and calls the near word the word of faith.

connections.label: Provoked to jealousy by a no-people
connections.explanation: In the Song of Moses God says that as Israel provoked him with what is not God, he will provoke them with those who are not a people. Paul quotes it, introducing it with First Moses says, and uses the Septuagint's two verbs (below).

connections.label: Vengeance is mine
connections.explanation: In the Song of Moses God declares that vengeance and recompense are his. Paul quotes the saying as written to tell the Romans not to avenge themselves but to leave room for God's wrath.

connections.label: I will never leave you
connections.explanation: As Moses hands over to Joshua, he tells Israel and Joshua that the LORD will not fail them or forsake them. Hebrews quotes the promise to urge contentment instead of love of money, with the Septuagint's verb for leaving (below).

connections.label: Remove the evil from among you
connections.explanation: Deuteronomy repeats the formula that Israel must remove the evil from among them. Paul closes his instruction about a case of immorality in Corinth with these words, and his verb, found nowhere else in the New Testament, is the Septuagint's (below).

connections.label: A consuming fire
connections.explanation: Moses warns Israel not to make images, because the LORD their God is a devouring fire, a jealous God. Hebrews ends its warning with the same words, our God is a consuming fire, and its participle, found nowhere else in the New Testament, is the Septuagint's (below).

connections.label: The commandments summed up
connections.explanation: Deuteronomy repeats the Ten Commandments, including those against adultery, murder, theft, false witness and coveting. Paul lists these commandments and says they are summed up in loving one's neighbour as oneself; his verbs are the Septuagint's (below).

connections.label: Cursed is anyone hanged on a tree
connections.explanation: Deuteronomy rules that the body of an executed man hung on a tree must not remain overnight, for he who is hanged is accursed of God. Paul quotes it to say that Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us.

connections.label: Two or three witnesses
connections.explanation: Deuteronomy requires that a matter be established by the mouth of two or three witnesses. Paul quotes the rule as he prepares for his third visit to Corinth; the word for witnesses is the Septuagint's (below).

connections.label: The walls of Jericho
connections.explanation: Israel marches around Jericho for seven days, the priests blow the trumpets, the people shout and the wall falls down flat. Hebrews counts this among the acts of faith, saying the walls fell after they had been encircled for seven days, with the Septuagint's verb for going around (below).

connections.label: Rahab spared at Jericho
connections.explanation: When Jericho falls, Joshua saves Rahab the prostitute and her household because she hid the spies. Hebrews names Rahab the prostitute among the examples of faith: she did not perish with the disobedient, because she had received the spies in peace (her name below as in the Septuagint).

connections.label: Rahab and the messengers
connections.explanation: Rahab hides Joshua's two spies in Jericho and lets them down by a cord through her window so that they escape another way. James names her as justified by her works, for welcoming the messengers and sending them off by a different road.

connections.label: If Joshua had given them rest
connections.explanation: Joshua reminds the tribes that the LORD is giving them rest and this land. Hebrews names Joshua and argues that if he had given the people rest, God would not have spoken later of another day, so a rest still remains; the verb is the Septuagint's in Joshua 1:13 (below).

connections.label: The land given as an inheritance
connections.explanation: Joshua 14 begins the account of how Israel's tribes received their inheritances in Canaan by lot. In the synagogue at Pisidian Antioch Paul retells Israel's story and says God destroyed seven nations in Canaan and gave the people their land as an inheritance.

connections.label: The ground Jacob gave to Joseph
connections.explanation: The book of Joshua ends with Joseph's bones buried at Shechem, in the parcel of ground Jacob had bought. John places the meeting with the Samaritan woman at Sychar, beside the plot of land Jacob had given Joseph; the names are as in the Septuagint (below).

connections.label: Buried at Shechem
connections.explanation: Joshua records that the bones of Joseph, brought up from Egypt, were buried at Shechem in ground bought from the sons of Hamor. Stephen tells the council that the fathers were brought back to Shechem and laid in the tomb bought from the children of Hamor.

connections.label: A son promised to a barren wife
connections.explanation: The LORD's angel tells Manoah's wife, barren and childless, that she will bear a son who will be set apart from the womb and that she must drink no wine nor strong drink. Gabriel tells Zechariah that his barren wife Elizabeth will bear a son who will drink no wine nor strong drink and be filled with the Holy Spirit from his mother's womb. Luke's word for barren is the Septuagint's in Judges 13 (below).

connections.label: Gideon
connections.explanation: The LORD's angel finds Gideon threshing wheat in hiding and sends him against Midian, which he routs with three hundred men and trumpets. Hebrews names Gideon first among those it has no time to tell of, who through faith became mighty in war; the name is spelled as in the Septuagint (below).

connections.label: Jephthah
connections.explanation: Jephthah the Gileadite, son of a prostitute and driven out by his brothers, is called back to lead Israel and defeats the Ammonites. Hebrews names Jephthah among the judges whose faith it has no time to recount (his name below as in the Septuagint).

connections.label: Samson
connections.explanation: Samson, promised before his birth, tears a lion apart when the Spirit comes on him and fights the Philistines to his death. Hebrews names Samson among those who through faith stopped the mouths of lions and out of weakness were made strong; name and lion are the Septuagint's words (below).

connections.label: Boaz, Ruth and the line of David
connections.explanation: Ruth ends with Boaz marrying Ruth, the birth of Obed, and a short genealogy down to David. Matthew's genealogy of Jesus names Boaz as the father of Obed by Ruth, then Obed, Jesse and King David, one of the few women named in it.

connections.label: The generations from Perez to David
connections.explanation: Ruth closes with the generations from Perez to David: Hezron, Ram, Amminadab, Nahshon, Salmon, Boaz, Obed and Jesse. Luke's genealogy of Jesus, read in the other direction, passes through the same names, with the Septuagint's spelling of Nahshon (below).

connections.label: Under his wings
connections.explanation: Boaz blesses Ruth in the name of the God of Israel, under whose wings she has come to take refuge. Lamenting over Jerusalem, Jesus says he longed to gather its children as a hen gathers her brood under her wings; the word for wings is the Septuagint's in Ruth 2:12 (below).
